Oil Sinks to $94 as Iran’s $8 Billion Hormuz Deal Heads to Trump
Brent crude fell 3.6% to $94.00 per barrel on Monday as Qatar's prime minister headed to the White House with an Iranian proposal for an interim deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. WTI dropped 3% to $88.09, and U.S. natural gas rose 0.8% to $3.02/MMBtu as of 7:26 a.m. ET. The decline extends last week's 16% slide in Brent, the benchmark's steepest weekly fall since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Iran has signed off on the Qatari-brokered terms, according to two diplomatic sources who spoke to Israeli media . Tehran would reopen Hormuz and halt attacks on Gulf tankers. Washington would lift its naval and economic blockade of Iran and release $8 billion in Iranian funds frozen in Qatar. Under the terms, Iran drops its demand to control the strait and charge transit fees but still refuses to put its nuclear program on the table. Neither government has confirmed the terms, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth reportedly oppose a deal along these lines.
Trump said on Sunday that renewed U.S. strikes on Iran are "highly unlikely" if negotiations produce a strong agreement. Rubio, speaking in Florida the same day, called Iran's demands "outrageous and ridiculous" and said the two sides are not close to a breakthrough. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz within two days stands, on condition that the war ends on all fronts.
Shipping through Hormuz came under fire again over the weekend, with Washington and Tehran both reporting attacks on vessels in or near the strait, and the Iran-aligned Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Aramco's offices in Riyadh on Sunday. Murban crude, the physical Gulf benchmark, climbed 3.4% to $99.17 in Asian trading. A similar U.S.-Iran memorandum reached in Switzerland in May collapsed after an Iranian attack on oil tankers in the strait.

Cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers has geopolitical context
‘Not particularly complex’ defrosting hack has been attributed to Iran, with presumption it is linked to others across Europe
In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.
There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.
France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.
An employee fills boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.
Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.
Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.
Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.
Boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters
Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?
“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.
The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.
However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

Chris Ward co-authored the red lines on the UK’s relationship with the EU in Labour’s 2024 manifesto. Photograph: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA
Labour’s Brexit red lines ready for ‘dignified retirement’, says their co-author
Exclusive: MP Chris Ward believes ditching pledges and forming closer ties with EU would protect it from global threats
One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for Andy Burnham to abandon them at the next election, saying a new relationship with the EU would protect the UK from global threats.
The call is the latest voice from a prominent figure in Starmer’s administration for a faster transition to a far closer European relationship, after the former chancellor Rachel Reeves said it was right for Burnham to consider rejoining .
No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement
Chris Ward, one of Starmer’s closest confidants in politics and one of the ministers who worked on the EU reset, said that it was the security relationship that meant a change was now imperative.
The Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven said it was now time to give a “a dignified retirement” to the red lines, which rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union and restoring freedom of movement .
Ward also suggested there was little compelling argument for rejoining the single market without full EU membership, saying he had “never understood the argument for the latter without the former”.
But he said the main reason for abandoning the red lines was that the UK “could no longer rely on the Americans” which was a major geopolitical shift that merited an entire reappraisal of Britain’s diplomatic relationships. “That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026,” he wrote in an article for the Guardian.
Ward, who was Starmer’s chief adviser as shadow Brexit secretary and who co-authored the red lines in Labour’s manifesto in 2024, said that they had now outlived their usefulness and should no longer be part of Labour’s future thinking.
Britain cannot deal effectively with geopolitical crises without rejoining EU, says thinktank
He remains close to the former prime minister and said that the drive to renew the relationship with the EU may prove the defining political moment of this autumn.
He said the party had agreed upon the red lines in the manifesto because they were “designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour”.
“I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at next month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.
“By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.”
Ward said it was well known that rejoining the EU or single market would have economic benefits but said supporters of rejoining should make a different argument.
“Pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what’s really changed,” he wrote.
“Instead, its the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of relationship.”
He said Starmer had twice had to scramble alliances together – on Ukraine and on the strait of Hormuz – because “we could no longer rely on the Americans”.
“It would now be brave in the extreme to continue to pin our future security – and that of Europe – on the outcome of US elections, or the false hope that whoever is in the White House we can still bank on the US as we did in 2016, let alone 1945.”
Ward said there should be public debate on whether the UK should formally rejoin or seek a form of associate membership like Canada.
But he said the prime minister will “need to be clear as to why now is the right time to reopen the Brexit debate, what we are seeking, and why it is so important to our national interest. A re-run of the tired arguments of 2016 won’t do that. Defending red lines designed for 2020 won’t do that either. But appreciating the urgent strategic challenges of the decades to come just might.”
Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, expected to be used to see Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.
Burnham will also meet European leaders on the sidelines to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to seek a closer and more permanent relationship – including potentially rejoining the bloc.
At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, the UK will sign new agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
The prime minister is then expected to give a speech after the summit on options for the future relationship. Burnham has said previously an option to rejoin the single market could be offered in a Labour manifesto but fully rejoining would need a referendum.

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot  gold and  silver prices were sharply higher in late U.S. trading Monday, supported by a weaker U.S. dollar and a steep decline in crude oil prices as investors responded to renewed hopes for a diplomatic resolution to the U.S.-Iran conflict. The retreat in energy prices eased some inflation concerns ahead of Tuesday's U.S. consumer price index report, although Friday's stronger-than-expected employment figures continued to support expectations for another Federal Reserve interest rate increase in December. A broad recovery in North American and European equity markets also reflected improving investor sentiment following last week's technology-led selloff. Spot gold was trading near $4,140.40 an ounce, up $69.40, or 1.70%, while spot silver was trading near $53.320, up $1.350, or 2.60%.
Gold extended its recovery following last week's sharp fluctuations, when Democrats' victories in the U.S. midterm elections initially drove Treasury yields and the dollar lower before stronger employment data revived expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening. Monday's decline in crude oil prices helped offset some of those monetary policy concerns, while the softer dollar improved the relative attractiveness of precious metals. Silver outperformed gold as the recovery in broader financial markets encouraged renewed buying interest.
The latest U.S. economic reports continue to indicate resilient labor-market conditions despite elevated borrowing costs and recent volatility in technology shares. Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report showed an increase of 165,000 jobs, substantially exceeding expectations for approximately 65,000. The unemployment rate declined to 4.1% from 4.2%, while average hourly earnings increased 0.4% on the month and 3.1% annually. August and September payroll figures were revised upward by a combined 84,000 jobs, reinforcing evidence that employment conditions remain stronger than previously estimated. The figures increased expectations that the Fed could raise interest rates again in December, even as financial-market volatility and declining energy prices complicate the inflation outlook.
Market positioning remains focused on Tuesday's October consumer price index report and the Federal Reserve's Dec. 8-9 policy meeting. Interest rate futures indicated approximately an 82.2% probability of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December in Monday's afternoon market assessment. That follows Friday's stronger employment figures, which reinforced expectations that the central bank will prioritize persistent inflation over concerns about slowing economic activity. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading near 4.86% in afternoon dealings, while the more policy-sensitive two-year yield was near 4.55%. Both remained elevated despite the decline in crude oil prices, reflecting continued uncertainty about the inflation outlook and future monetary policy.
The U.S. dollar weakened Monday after Friday's strong rally, providing additional support for gold and silver. The dollar index declined approximately 0.3% toward 101.88 during the session, as improving equity-market sentiment and reduced concerns about an immediate escalation involving Iran encouraged investors to reduce some defensive currency positions. However, the dollar's retreat remained limited by expectations for higher U.S. interest rates. The combination of falling energy prices, elevated Treasury yields and a softer dollar highlights the competing influences shaping precious metals positioning ahead of Tuesday's inflation figures.
The Labor Department will release the October consumer price index Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. EST. Economists expect headline consumer prices to increase approximately 0.3% on the month, following a 0.6% rise in September. Investors will pay particular attention to core inflation, which excludes food and energy, for evidence that underlying price pressures are moderating. A softer-than-expected report could reduce December rate increase expectations and push Treasury yields and the dollar lower, providing additional support for gold. Conversely, stronger inflation would reinforce the implications of Friday's employment surprise and could trigger renewed selling in precious metals as traders increase expectations for further tightening.
The week's remaining economic calendar includes Thursday's weekly initial jobless claims report at 8:30 a.m. EST and Friday's October producer price index at 8:30 a.m. EST. Federal Reserve officials are also expected to provide further commentary on inflation and labor-market developments. U.S. Treasury markets will be closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, while stock markets remain open. Investors will also monitor Treasury auctions and corporate earnings for indications of demand for government debt and the outlook for technology-sector investment. Continued volatility in artificial intelligence-related equities could encourage defensive demand for gold, although higher yields or broader portfolio liquidation remain potential constraints.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major influence on global commodity markets Monday as President Donald Trump downplayed the possibility of renewed large-scale military strikes against Iran while negotiations toward a settlement continue. His comments encouraged traders to reduce the geopolitical risk premium embedded in crude oil prices, extending the steep losses recorded during the previous week. However, the prospect of a diplomatic settlement remains uncertain, with both Washington and Tehran continuing to report attacks involving shipping in or near the strategic waterway.
Crude oil prices plunged Monday as traders increasingly considered the possibility of reduced military tensions and improved petroleum shipments. Brent crude futures settled down $5.75, or 5.85%, at $92.57 a barrel, while Nymex WTI crude futures declined $3.98, or 4.38%, to settle at $86.85. Both benchmarks extended their losses in post-settlement trading, with Brent falling more than $7 a barrel at one point and reaching its lowest level since late August. The decline followed a roughly 16% weekly loss in Brent, reflecting the rapid removal of some of the geopolitical risk premium accumulated during the conflict.
For gold, lower energy prices have reduced some inflation concerns and encouraged expectations that the Federal Reserve may have less reason to maintain an extended tightening cycle. However, the immediate outlook remains complicated by resilient employment, persistent underlying inflation and elevated Treasury yields. The continuing uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz also supports underlying defensive demand, even as the prospect of diplomatic progress reduces the urgency of geopolitical hedging. Silver has benefited from the broader recovery in precious metals, although its industrial exposure leaves it sensitive to manufacturing demand, financing conditions and the direction of global economic activity.
North American equity markets rallied sharply Monday as falling crude oil prices, improving risk sentiment and renewed buying in technology shares helped markets recover from last week's steep losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to close at 52,389.75. The S&P 500 advanced 173.08 points, or 2.35%, to finish at 7,549.94, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 673.71 points, or 2.74%, to close at 25,253.14. The Russell 2000 outperformed the major benchmarks, climbing 86.71 points, or 3.15%, to 2,840.81. Monday's advance marked the strongest overall U.S. equity session since April, as investors reassessed the implications of lower energy costs for inflation, corporate profitability and interest rates.
Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also finished sharply higher Monday, advancing approximately 1.84% to around 36,450, supported by gains in mining, financial and industrial shares. Precious metals producers benefited from firmer bullion prices, while banks and other economically sensitive companies participated in the broader North American equity recovery. Energy shares underperformed as crude oil prices declined. Barrick Mining gained approximately 4.5% following its quarterly earnings announcement, while Greenfire Resources surged after Strathcona Resources announced plans to acquire the company. The advance extended Friday's recovery, when the Canadian benchmark gained 0.52% to close at 35,789.09.
European equity markets also closed firmly higher Monday as lower energy prices, stronger bank earnings and renewed buying in technology shares supported a broad-based recovery. The pan-European Stoxx 600 gained 1.26% to close at 656.52, while Germany's DAX advanced 1.73% to 26,267.19. France's CAC 40 rose 1.16% to 8,233.30, and the U.K.'s FTSE 100 climbed 1.02% to 10,782.87. Spain's IBEX 35 increased 1.93% to 19,742.50, while Italy's FTSE MIB led the major European benchmarks with a 2.69% gain to 51,399.88.

items.content:
Perished food outside supermarkets hit by cyber-attacks targeting refrigeration systems in France. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters
Perished food outside supermarkets hit by cyber-attacks targeting refrigeration systems in France. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters
Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says
French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month
France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”.
Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”.
At a press briefing during the G7 summit in Paris, he said: “Thanks to the remarkable efforts of government agencies, I am able to confirm that the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are responsible for this attack.”
He said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned “to protest in the strongest possible terms against this extremely serious act.”
Swathes of French supermarkets were hit in the cyber-attacks on 11 and 12 October. Some were forced to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.
Similar incidents have been reported since, including on supermarket fridges in other European countries last week and on a French blood bank.
The Paris public prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said on Monday that specialist investigators and government agencies had identified “a modus operandi” characteristic of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, a cyber warfare unit linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
This included “the use of Farsi and IP addresses traced back to devices located in Iran”, she said.
Beccuau said her office had opened a investigation against the head of Shahid Kaveh, his deputies and “others who will be identified” on charges of “fraudulent attacks on an automated data processing system committed as part of an organised crime ring and of causing damage dangerous to persons”.
She said the offences were “aggravated by the fact they were committed to serve a foreign power – in this case Iran”.
Gérôme Billois, a partner at the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said Shahid Kaveh had been active since 2020 and was known to have carried out cyber-attacks mostly on water distribution systems in the US.
“Two countries are known for this kind of attack: Iran and Russia. Given that recent cyber-attacks on supermarkets and the blood bank in France concerned freezers it is reasonable to think Iran is directly linked to both,” he said,
“For the moment they are attacking easy equipment but as a state group that has the means, the determination and the time, we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity.”
During the attack last month, hackers remotely overrode the temperature setting on thousands of freezers , fridges and chiller cabinets in as many as 700 supermarkets and shops across France, pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F) in some cases.
Thousands of tons of food had to be dumped and in some stores the extreme temperature rise sparked fires, triggering sprinklers and water damage.
Hackers last week accessed control systems at cold stores stocking blood products. The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds and been raised to “very high level” but that technicians had been alerted by alarm systems allowing them to disconnect the cold stores before the products were destroyed. It is not clear whether the two attacks are linked.
The following day retailers in 11 European countries including the UK, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with refrigeration systems.
A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank also reported losing more than €100m in a cyber-attack on Friday. The bank said it had recuperated some of the money.
The European Commission did not immediately comment on the French foreign minister’s statement. Kaja Kallas, the head of foreign affairs for the EU said: “We have the foreign affairs council next Monday, so we will have the opportunity to discuss this. These cyber incidents occurring in Europe, if attributed [to Iran], also call for a strong response on our part.”
In a significant decision this year, the EU designated the IRGC a terrorist organisation , ending years of division over the issue. The designation became possible after France dropped its long-held opposition, having previously feared it would damage diplomatic channels and the interests of French nationals in Iran.

items.title: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
items.summary: The discount chain is continuing to edge towards collapse and is said to be "running on fumes", according to one insider.
items.content:
By Emma Simpson ,Â  Business correspondent Â  and Â  Simon Jack ,Â  Business editor
Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.
The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal.
About Â£50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.
Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for Â£1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.
Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday.
Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.
Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was Â£1.5m ahead of budget.
He said the business made a profit of Â£18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of Â£68m.
Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators
However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture of the business, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
It has also made Â£18m, from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers will appear before the Business Select Committee with MPs probing whether they are genuinely pursuing a solvent rescue of the business, which has 11,000 employees, and whether every realistic step is being taken to protect jobs and stores.
The session is being held in private given commercially sensitive discussions are still under way with bidders.
On Thursday, the 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.
If not, Poundland is set to collapse into administration and could be broken up.
A source familiar with the sales process said London-based Xyra Group was making "significant progress" in its last minute bid to buy Poundland and could now be the front runner.
An extension of Thursday's deadline now seems an increasingly likely scenario. But such a case would be difficult to put forward if Gordon Brothers continues to block funding.
One observer remarked "if Gordon Brothers is going in front of that committee, you don't want to be giving the message we're pulling up the drawbridge".
Even if a deal is agreed to sell the business as a whole, there is no guarantee a new owner would not reduce the number of stores, but suppliers to Poundland would prefer that outcome to hundreds of sites being sold off to other retailers.
There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up stores which could mean continuing employment for many workers.
The central issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland trading as a national chain.

NVIDIA Allegedly Became A Roadblock For Federal Investigation In Megaspeed AI Chip Smuggling Probe After GPU Maker Intervened With Commerce Department
The political storm engulfing NVIDIA continues to intensify as the report discusses in detail how deep corporate maneuvering collided with federal law enforcement. The AI GPU manufacturer is probably already wrestling with the independent board inquiry  following CEO Jensen Huang’s admitted relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Now, we learn that NVIDIA became a thorn in an ongoing federal investigation into AI chip smuggling. More specifically, the probe involved Megaspeed, the same company whose Chinese executive, Alice Huang, is said to have been involved in espionage and an affair with NVIDIA’s CEO.
Agents did demonstrate resistance during the probe, but it was all for naught as the inquiry was handed over to the DOJ
Shortly after reporting on NVIDIA’s high-end H200 AI GPUs found in China’s ghost offices , The New York Times has returned, this time, with a focus on Megaspeed. Federal scrutiny had converged on the Singapore-based data center outfit led by Alice Huang, with U.S. intelligence agencies concluding that she was operating as an intelligence asset on behalf of Beijing, while simultaneously developing an intimate relationship with NVIDIA’s Chief Executive Officer.
Related Story NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang Expected To Weather Independent Board Probe As Analysts Give An 87% Probability Of Retaining CEO Role
Export enforcement officials had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was functioning as a multi-billion-dollar front to smuggle embargoed NVIDIA AI accelerators past trade controls and directly into mainland China. Unfortunately, the investigation hit an impregnable wall in 2025, with the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security receiving direct correspondence from Tim Teter, NVIDIA’s General Counsel.
While it’s considered standard practice for corporate attorneys to interface with regulatory agencies regarding compliance matters, the nature of Teter’s communication set off immediate alarm bells inside the department. Teter specifically claimed that Jeff Kessler, a top political appointee nominated by President Trump, had granted NVIDIA explicit authorization to reach out directly regarding the probe.
Kessler’s name certainly caught the authorities off guard, with several officials reportedly viewing NVIDIA’s intervention as a gross violation of standard protocol that threatened to taint the entire enforcement action. However, rather than complying, the officials escalated the matter internally, only for the inquiry to stall and ultimately be transferred away from the Commerce Department over to the Department of Justice.
What’s surprising is Kessler’s supposed hypocritical stance, believing that agents should proceed strictly by the book, but at the same time, the intervention severely undercut the operational momentum of the investigators. Also, given Jensen Huang’s infidelity and the timing of this report, NVIDIA’s CEO should brace himself for a firestorm during his imminent closed-door congressional briefing on November 18 .
As far as removing Huang from his executive position goes, the majority of analysts cannot seem to paint a picture where NVIDIA’s head honcho will be replaced . However, given that in less than 48 hours, we’ve stumbled upon a goldmine of surprises, you never know what the latest development might materialize, so stay tuned.

A lot of AI chip stocks on the Nasdaq have fallen significantly in recent months. Believe it or not, many names in this space are now down more than 50% from their 2026 highs.
Could we be looking at a golden buying opportunity? Let's discuss.
Many of the AI chip stocks peaked around late June. Since then, the trend has generally been down .
We can see this in the iShares Semiconductor ETF . It hit an all-time high on 22 June and has since fallen almost 40%.
Zooming in on individual chip names, the losses have been much larger in many cases. Memory stock SanDisk , for example, has fallen from $2,355 to $835 – a decline of 65%.
Chip manufacturing equipment specialist Lam Research is another name worth highlighting. It has dropped from $439 to $200 – a fall of 54%.
Personally, I reckon there's a golden buying opportunity after such falls. And I'm not just saying that – I've been buying chip stocks for my own portfolio over the last week.
Sure, there are risks around a slowdown in data centre spending. Especially after the Democrats secured victory in the midterm elections in the US.
But the way I see it, AI is here to stay – the genie isn't going back in the bottle. To my mind, data centres will continue to be built, whether it's in the US or somewhere else.
And I reckon valuations in the chip space are now looking attractive, particularly after the extreme falls across the sector last week. Taking a three-to-five year view, I see the potential for attractive returns.
One position I added to last week was KLA Corp ( NASDAQ: KLAC ). It specialises in process control and yield management solutions for the chip industry so it's essentially a 'picks-and-shovels' play on the sector.
Back in late June, it was trading above $300. Last week, however, I was able to buy some shares just above $150.
At that price, the stock was trading on a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 24, falling to 19 using next year's earnings forecast. I think that's good value for this name.
Because not only does it play a crucial role in the chip sector but it's also highly profitable. Additionally, it's growing at a strong rate – recent Q1 earnings showed year-on-year revenue growth of 29%.
"The September quarter reflected continued strength in KLA's leading market position in process control as growing semiconductor complexity drives more stringent requirements. US Stock Futures Advance as Oil Prices Slide and Investors Await Inflation Report: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
New York Stock Exchange trading floor ©Scott Bealse US equity futures indicated gains ahead of Monday's opening bell, supported by a decline in crude oil prices as markets attempted to build on Friday's recovery following the previous session's technology-sector sell-off.
American crude futures dropped more than 4% after President Donald Trump suggested that additional military action against Iran was "highly unlikely" while diplomatic discussions continued over the country's nuclear programme and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
However, Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed reservations about the negotiations, describing Iran's demands as "outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic."
The developments contributed to movements in energy prices as investors prepared for economic releases and corporate earnings announcements later in the week.
Nasdaq Rebounds but Technology Sector Faces Further Uncertainty
Technology shares were positioned for further gains following Friday's recovery, although Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) declined more than 5% in premarket trading.
The chipmaker said it would investigate reports alleging that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
Friday's session saw the Nasdaq Composite increase 1.1%, or 264.43 points, to 24,579.42. The S&P 500 gained 23.13 points, or 0.3%, to finish at 7,376.86.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved in the opposite direction, falling 237.33 points, or 0.5%, to 51,285.73.
For the week, the Nasdaq recorded a 3.4% decline, while the S&P 500 lost 2.7% and the Dow retreated 0.9%.
The earlier sell-off had pushed the Nasdaq to its lowest closing level in more than six months and the S&P 500 to a three-month low.
Semiconductor and Networking Stocks Lead Friday's Recovery
Semiconductor companies contributed to the market rebound, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index advancing 4.2% after a 12.3% decline during Thursday's session.
Networking stocks also gained ground, reflected in a 4.1% increase in the NYSE Arca Networking Index.
Elsewhere, the NYSE Arca Gold Bugs Index rose 2.6% despite a decline in gold prices.
Airline and oilfield services shares also advanced, while housing-related stocks recorded losses.
The sector movements followed Thursday's market decline, with investors reassessing equity valuations ahead of additional economic data.
US labour market figures showed that non-farm employment increased by 165,000 positions in October, considerably above economists' expectations for 62,000 additional jobs.
The Labor Department also revised employment figures for the preceding two months upwards by a combined 84,000 positions.
August payroll growth was revised to 186,000, while September employment gains were adjusted to 60,000.
The unemployment rate decreased to 4.1% from 4.2% in September, compared with forecasts for an unchanged reading.
Michael Pearce, Chief US Economist at Oxford Economics, said the employment figures suggested tighter labour market conditions and strengthened the case for a December interest rate increase.
"The latest jobs data suggest labor market conditions are tightening, and with inflation well above target, that adds to the case for a December rate hike," Pearce said.
He also noted that further declines in technology shares and energy prices could reduce inflationary pressures and remove the need for another rate increase in early 2027.
Consumer Sentiment Rises Ahead of Inflation Figures
Preliminary figures from the University of Michigan indicated that US consumer sentiment improved in November.
The university's sentiment index increased to 51.0 from 48.0 in October, exceeding economists' expectations for no change.
The improvement followed a period of volatility in financial markets, while employment figures continued to influence expectations for Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Investors will now assess forthcoming inflation data and corporate earnings reports for further indications of the direction of US interest rates and economic activity.

Nasdaq Stock Market Correction: 3 AI Stocks You Can Buy Right Now and Hold Forever
When most investors think about a stock market correction, they think about fear, and this past Thursday had plenty of it. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Nov. 5, leaving it 12% below its Oct. 6 record close and officially in correction territory.
Chip stocks took the worst of it. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 12% in a single day, on fears that the new Democratic majority in Congress will slow the build-out of AI data centers.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Let's be clear. Although it's certainly not fun to watch the value of your investments plunge, corrections like this are a normal part of investing, even if they never feel that way. And it's important to emphasize that nothing has actually changed about AI demand, and no new rules have been enacted. That's why I think the sell-off created a buying opportunity in three of the most notable AI leaders.
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is an AI stock that needs no introduction, but it hasn't been this cheap in a while. In its most recent quarter, revenue more than doubled, up 106% year over year to more than $96 billion, and data center revenue grew 117% to $89 billion. Management guided for about $108 billion in revenue for the current quarter, and that forecast assumes no data center revenue from China. Gross margin was 75%, which shows Nvidia still has enormous pricing power.
Even so, the stock closed at $181.60 on Thursday, 24% below its October record, and trades for less than 16 times forward earnings. Nvidia is also putting its cash to work, with a $235 billion total buyback authorization following a $150 billion increase in September. The next big test comes on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports its third-quarter results, but this could be an opportunity to add the chipmaking leader to your portfolio at a discount.
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) designs custom AI chips for some of the world's largest tech companies, as well as the networking gear that connects them. Its AI semiconductor revenue soared 221% year over year to $16.7 billion last quarter, and management expects that number to reach $21.7 billion this quarter. CEO Hock Tan said demand for custom AI accelerators and networking "continues to be very strong."
Despite that, Broadcom fell more than 10% on Thursday and is roughly 40% below its June record close. At about 17 times forward earnings, with $13.7 billion in quarterly free cash flow and a growing dividend, it's one of the more reasonably priced ways to own AI infrastructure. Total revenue is expected to grow 93% this quarter to about $34.8 billion, which is incredible growth, especially for a company of Broadcom's size.
AMD's (NASDAQ:AMD) drop during the market sell-off was especially hard to watch. Just two days earlier, AMD reported 45% revenue growth, guided well above expectations for the fourth quarter, and said it expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. The stock still fell 17% on Thursday and is now more than 30% below its record close, even after a significant rebound on Friday.
In other words, the business looks stronger than ever, and the stock is much more attractive than it was a month ago. Unlike the other two, AMD isn't a cheap stock, still trading at about 37 times forward earnings, but it also has a larger market opportunity ahead, so its growth rate could be sustainable for years to come.
To be sure, if the sell-off's premise proves correct and data center construction slows meaningfully, all three companies would feel it. Volatility is also likely to stay high, especially heading into Nvidia's report. But I'd rather buy great businesses (which will still be great businesses, even if the data center boom slows) after a policy scare than after a run to all-time highs.
Having said all that, corrections are a normal part of investing, and they often create the best opportunities to buy great companies. Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD all just showed that AI demand is still accelerating. For long-term investors, Thursday's sell-off looks more like an opportunity than a warning.

US Stock Futures Mixed as Investors Assess Berkshire Hathaway Earnings, Nvidia Reports and AI Regulation Plans: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
US stock futures were mixed on Monday, November 9, 2026, as investors prepared for inflation data, corporate earnings and developments affecting the technology and cryptocurrency sectors.
At 3:42 a.m. Eastern Time, S&P 500 futures were up 0.35%, while Nasdaq 100 futures declined 0.3%. Dow Jones futures advanced 0.6%.
Market attention centred on reports involving Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) Chief Executive Jensen Huang, a leadership change at Binance following a reported cryptocurrency security breach, and third-quarter results from Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRK.B).
Investors were also awaiting earnings from CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) and Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO), alongside US consumer inflation figures.
Proposed legislation concerning artificial intelligence and data-centre development added another consideration for technology companies.
Nvidia Shares Decline Following Unverified Reports Concerning CEO
Nvidia shares fell more than 4% in premarket trading on Monday following reports concerning Chief Executive Jensen Huang.
The reports alleged that Huang had acknowledged an extramarital relationship in a communication to employees and that Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation.
The source also included allegations concerning the possible involvement of foreign intelligence services. These claims have not been independently substantiated, and the available information does not establish that the reported investigation or intelligence-related allegations are accurate.
A memorandum attributed to Huang included the following statement:
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
The authenticity of the reported memorandum has not been independently established.
The allegations have attracted attention because of Huang's leadership role at Nvidia, a major supplier of semiconductor technology used in artificial intelligence systems.
The reported premarket decline followed a period of volatility in the company's shares.
Binance Announces CFO Departure Following Reported $6.3 Billion Cryptocurrency Theft
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance announced that Chief Financial Officer Kaiser Ng would leave the company to pursue another business opportunity.
The announcement followed reports of a cybersecurity breach involving approximately $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency.
According to Binance, Ng's departure had been planned for several months and was not presented as a consequence of the reported security incident.
Co-Chief Executive Yi He said the finance executive had decided to leave after more than five years with the company, with a transition process underway for approximately six months.
Justin Yek, previously vice-president of finance at Airwallex, has been named as Ng's successor.
The reported security breach occurred on October 29 and allegedly involved malware distributed through software downloads and fraudulent recruitment activity targeting engineering employees.
The source attributed the theft to a North Korean hacking group, citing the FBI, while stating that North Korea had denied responsibility. These claims have not been independently verified.
Binance has said it intends to reimburse affected customers in full.
The company has not disclosed additional financial details concerning the reimbursement process in the supplied report.
Berkshire Hathaway Operating Earnings Fall 5.8% as Cash Reaches $377.4 Billion
Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRK.B) reported a 5.8% year-on-year decline in third-quarter operating earnings, primarily reflecting lower results from its insurance operations.
Operating earnings decreased to $12.7 billion from $13.48 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year.
The operating earnings measure excludes certain investment-related gains and losses that can influence reported net income.
Berkshire's cash holdings increased to a record $377.4 billion during the quarter.
The conglomerate also repurchased approximately $9.6 billion of its own shares over the reporting period.
The combination of higher cash reserves and share repurchases provides information about the company's capital allocation during the quarter.
The reported results indicate that Berkshire maintained substantial liquidity despite the decline in operating earnings.
US Inflation Report and Technology Earnings in Focus
Investors were preparing for the publication of the October US Consumer Price Index report, scheduled for Tuesday.
The inflation figures will provide an update on consumer price movements and may influence expectations concerning the Federal Reserve's future interest-rate decisions.
Financial markets will assess the figures against forecasts, particularly for indications of whether inflationary pressures are moderating or persisting.
Corporate earnings will also remain in focus, with several technology companies scheduled to publish results.
CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) and Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) are among the companies expected to report.
Their results could provide additional information about spending on cloud computing, semiconductor equipment and networking infrastructure.
These businesses operate in areas connected to investment in artificial intelligence technology, making their financial performance relevant to assessments of corporate technology expenditure.
Democrats Consider New Artificial Intelligence and Data-Centre Regulations
US Democratic lawmakers are reportedly preparing legislative proposals concerning artificial intelligence and data-centre development ahead of an anticipated change in congressional control in January.
According to the supplied report, the proposals would address consumer electricity costs associated with data-centre expansion, independent testing of advanced AI systems and potential liability for damage caused by AI products.
The proposed measures would introduce additional regulatory requirements for some companies developing or operating artificial intelligence systems.
The report contrasted the proposals with the approach taken by Republican lawmakers, who have generally favoured measures supporting AI development.
However, any legislation would need to pass the relevant congressional procedures and obtain the necessary approvals.
President Donald Trump has opposed mandatory federal AI regulations, according to the report, creating a potential obstacle to the proposed legislation.
The measures remain under consideration and have not been enacted.
US stock futures showed differing movements ahead of the opening session, with gains in S&P 500 and Dow Jones futures contrasting with a decline in Nasdaq 100 futures.
Investors were assessing Berkshire Hathaway's quarterly earnings and record cash holdings, developments involving Nvidia and Binance, and potential changes to US artificial intelligence regulation.
The forthcoming inflation report and technology earnings announcements will provide further information about economic conditions and corporate performance.

Google's chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia's own AI boom
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is investigating its own CEO. Google ( GOOGL ) is busy building the chips that could take Nvidia's customers.
Nvidia fell more than 4% Monday to its lowest close since April 7 as its board looks into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy . That came even as chip stocks rallied, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) up more than 7%. Alphabet rose about 1%. It's the latest chapter in Wall Street's first $4.5 trillion CEO scandal .
Google introduced two new tensor processing units, or TPUs — its homegrown AI chips — on Monday. The TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max join the 8t and 8i it unveiled in April, the first time Google has introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Both new chips ship next year.
Think of it as a chip menu. The 8tx keeps data encrypted for governments, banks, and other regulated businesses, paired with processors from AMD ( AMD ). The 8i Max squeezes two chips into one package for requests with long context windows — the amount of information an AI model can juggle at once.
The forecasts are the eye-popper. Bloomberg Intelligence sees TPU sales rising from about $12 billion this year to more than $135 billion by 2028, not counting chips rented through Google Cloud. That's more than 11-fold in two years.
Nvidia's data center business grew nearly eightfold in the first two years of the AI boom, from $15 billion in fiscal 2023 to $115 billion in fiscal 2025.
Nvidia, Bloomberg Intelligence, Yahoo Finance The chips are already flying off the line. Epoch AI estimates TPU shipments doubled in computing power in a single quarter this year, to roughly 800,000 chips.
Anthropic is the headliner. Its IPO filing shows about $161 billion of lease payments tied to TPUs, which Raymond James says makes it the biggest custom-chip customer of Google's design partner, Broadcom ( AVGO ). Meta ( META ), OpenAI and Oracle ( ORCL ) are buyers too.
Google used to roll out about one data center TPU a year. Now it has one for every job.
Google, Yahoo Finance Nvidia still has the bigger engine.
Its next-generation Rubin chip is rated at 35 petaflops — a measure of raw computing speed — compared with about 10 for Google's 8i and about 20 for the 8i Max, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Google is selling on price. SemiAnalysis found that Google's current Ironwood TPU delivers up to nearly three times as much AI output per dollar as Nvidia's Blackwell chips when running AI agents, though Nvidia's top system still wins when speed is everything.
Google, Nvidia, AMD, Yahoo Finance Forecasts aren't sales, and Nvidia still sells far more AI chips than anyone else.
Nvidia's next big moment comes Nov. 17, when it reports third quarter results, a day before a requested closed-door House briefing on CEO Jensen Huang . Investors will want to hear whether customers are hedging their bets. As Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon wrote to clients, "Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS NVIDIA."

Google is introducing two new variations of its tensor processing units, or TPUs, designed to address growing demand for confidential computing and AI applications that need to process larger amounts of information, Bloomberg News reported Monday.
The new TPU 8tx and 8i Max offerings are designed for different workloads, reflecting Google's view that the next phase of artificial intelligence will require increasingly specialized hardware.
The TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential computing, with potential applications among government agencies and companies operating in regulated industries. The system also incorporates chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc., as part of a collaboration between the two companies.
The 8i Max, meanwhile, is designed to run AI applications requiring longer context windows, allowing models to consider substantially more information when responding to queries. Such capabilities are particularly relevant for drug discovery, mathematical applications and coding tools.
Neither offering represents an entirely new silicon design. Instead, Google has reconfigured its existing hardware to address specific requirements emerging from customers, according to Bloomberg.
"This really follows the thesis that we have here at Google, which is that the future is going to be about specialization, and the upsides for specialization continue to be significant," Google chip chief Amin Vahdat told Bloomberg.
The announcement marks an acceleration in Google's chip development. The company previously introduced a new generation of AI processors roughly every two years, but this year unveiled two generations of specialized processors simultaneously, with the latest variations expanding the lineup further.
Google gains ground as Nvidia faces fresh uncertainty
The timing is notable for the semiconductor industry, where Nvidia's dominance is facing increasing competition from companies developing their own AI accelerators.

Google has emerged as one of the most credible challengers, benefiting from years of internal chip development and growing interest from AI developers seeking alternatives to Nvidia's processors.
The opportunity extends beyond Google's own AI operations. Demand for computing capacity remains substantial, while the emergence of AI agents is creating new requirements for inference, memory and security. Specialized processors could allow customers to optimize performance and costs for particular workloads rather than relying on general-purpose solutions.
Nvidia, meanwhile, continues to benefit from demand that exceeds available supply, leaving considerable room for competitors to establish businesses without necessarily displacing the market leader.
But the company faces a separate challenge Monday following reports that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation.
Nvidia's board announced Sunday that it would launch an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed a report concerning his relationship with a business executive whom US authorities reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.
Huang also acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, apologizing to his family and colleagues.
Nvidia said its board had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership. The CEO has pledged to cooperate with the investigation.
The controversy is weighing on Nvidia shares, which were down 5.70% Monday, while Alphabet shares were up 2.4%.
The divergence reflects two separate developments: Google's expanding ambitions in AI infrastructure and the unexpected leadership and reputational uncertainty confronting Nvidia.
For Alphabet, the latest TPU expansion strengthens its position in a market that could become increasingly fragmented as AI workloads evolve. For Nvidia, the immediate concern is less about losing its technological lead overnight than maintaining investor confidence in a business whose extraordinary growth has been closely associated with Huang's leadership.
Google still has a considerable distance to travel before matching Nvidia's scale and software ecosystem. But its latest move underscores that competition in AI semiconductors is increasingly about offering the right processor for each task, rather than simply producing the most powerful chip.

Google Expands AI Chip Portfolio as Nvidia Faces Investigation Involving CEO
Alphabet Inc.'s Google (NASDAQ:GOOG) is expanding its artificial intelligence processor portfolio with two new configurations of its tensor processing units (TPUs), targeting specialised computing requirements as competition with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) continues to develop.
According to Bloomberg, Google is introducing the TPU 8tx and 8i Max, designed for confidential computing and AI applications requiring the processing of larger amounts of information.
The announcement comes as Nvidia faces an independent investigation concerning reports that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
The TPU 8tx is designed for confidential computing applications, including potential use by government organisations and businesses operating in regulated industries.
The system incorporates technology from Advanced Micro Devices as part of a collaboration between Google and the semiconductor manufacturer.
Meanwhile, the TPU 8i Max targets AI applications requiring longer context windows, allowing models to process more information when generating responses.
Potential applications include pharmaceutical research, mathematical computing and software development.
Bloomberg reported that neither product uses an entirely new chip architecture. Instead, Google has adapted existing hardware to address specific customer requirements.
Amin Vahdat, Google's head of chip development, explained the company's approach.
"This really follows the thesis that we have here at Google, which is that the future is going to be about specialization, and the upsides for specialization continue to be significant," he told Bloomberg.
Google's latest additions follow an increase in the pace of its AI processor development.
The company previously introduced new processor generations approximately every two years but has accelerated its development schedule, including the introduction of two generations of specialised processors during 2026.
The expansion reflects demand for computing infrastructure capable of supporting different AI workloads, including inference, automated agents and applications requiring additional memory or security.
Nvidia remains a major supplier of AI accelerators, although companies developing their own processors are introducing alternatives for specific computing requirements.
Separately, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
The announcement followed reports concerning Huang's relationship with a business executive whom US authorities reportedly suspected of gathering information for China.
Huang acknowledged marital infidelity in a message to employees and apologised to his family and colleagues.
Nvidia stated that its board had no reason to believe national security information or company secrets had been compromised and reaffirmed its confidence in Huang's leadership.
The chief executive has agreed to cooperate with the investigation.
Nvidia shares fell 5.70% on Monday following the reports, while Alphabet gained 2.4%.
The contrasting share price movements coincided with Google's processor announcements and the investigation involving Nvidia's chief executive.
Google's additional TPU configurations broaden its range of AI infrastructure products, while Nvidia continues to operate in a market characterised by substantial demand for computing capacity.
The developments highlight ongoing changes in the AI semiconductor industry as manufacturers introduce processors designed for increasingly specialised applications.

items.content:
San Francisco Fed president warns American workers face a treadmill of high inflation as wages fail to keep pace
San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said the central bank will likely need to raise interest rates further, warning that American workers remain trapped in what she called a "treadmill of high inflation" despite October's jobs report outpacing Wall Street expectations.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported the US economy added 165,000 jobs in October , nearly triple the Dow Jones consensus estimate, while the unemployment rate edged to 4.1%.
In a live CNBC interview , Daly separated the headline figures from the financial reality facing households.
"My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further. Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in," she said.
"More is likely to be needed, and certainly ... I'm prepared to do that if that's what the economy calls for."
Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% annually in October, below the latest consumer price index reading of 3.7% recorded in September . That means real wages are declining for much of the workforce even as job creation remains solid.
"They see that they can get jobs, they continue to spend. They're not out of the game, but they are on a treadmill of high inflation," Daly said.
"This has been high for too long, almost six years, and we're really starting to feel the burden of that spread everywhere."
The view aligns with that of Mike Fratantoni, chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) in Washington, DC, who shared at the MBA's annual convention in Chicago in October that "your typical household, their income is not keeping up with the cost of living. If you're going to watch one macroeconomic variable, I'd recommend this one, because I think that personal saving rate captures the whole story pretty well."
A powerful El Niño weather event could add as much as 1% to US consumer prices over the course of 2027, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. https://t.co/69yIoY9HOR
— Mortgage Professional America Magazine (@MPAMagazineUS) November 4, 2026
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised its benchmark rate to a target range of 3.75%-4% at the September meeting, the first rate hike since 2023 , before holding at the following gathering, citing a preference to wait for "the accumulation of more information."
Daly, who will vote on the FOMC next year, acknowledged a volatile broader backdrop, including the "painful" but orderly repricing of technology stocks, as a reason for the Fed to remain deliberate.
"Those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there," she said.
For mortgage brokers navigating a compressed market, the Fed's uncertain path extends the pressure.
The MBA projects two more rate hikes, one in December and another in the first quarter of 2027, with the 30-year mortgage rate expected to stay above 7% well into next year. Oxford Economics also backs a December Federal Reserve rate hike .
Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin separately said he also expects higher rates, but offered no firm timeline.

items.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
items.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Moment Thomas Massie introduces articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.
"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.
The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record.
"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."
He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.
Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.
"I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections.
He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power.
"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."
Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January.
Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that".
He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject.
Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office.
Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed.
As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.
The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.
While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago.
He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years.
Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority.
Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins.
"There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said.
Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.
While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term.
When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office.

Image caption, Trump has previously cast doubt on the integrity of US election results
US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.
Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.
Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing.
The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
"We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported," he said.
Stewart added that in some states, like Florida and Georgia, some initial reporting of results happens quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots.
Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
Surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi.
"State laws and practicalities are such that some states will just take longer to count," said Ruth Greenwood, director of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School.
"That doesn't mean anything nefarious is occurringâwe just need to trust local election officials to count every vote and tell us the results when they are done."
The outcome has been clear since election night. Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."
He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat.
"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said.
Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.
In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.
He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.
The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.
Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.
Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.
Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.
Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

items.title: At least 39 die after Europe-bound migrant boat sinks off Senegal
items.summary: The Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands remains dangerous for migrants seeking a better life
items.content:
Image caption, Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders estimates that for every 100 people who reach the Canary Islands by sea, 21 die during the crossing (file photo)
By Ondiro Oganga Â  and Â  Madina Maishanu ,Â  BBC Africa
At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports.
The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.
Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.
Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.
Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa.
Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.
The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.
Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.
