Share Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta closes citing gov’t clampdown on social media
Journalists from Novaya Gazeta take part in a farewell action outside their editorial office in Moscow, November 9, 2026 [Maxim Shipenkov/EPA]
Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta has ended operations due to pressure from authorities.
The newspaper reported that it held its last editorial meeting on Monday and closed its newsroom. It announced last month that it was being forced to shut down after being classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Why the Kremlin fears even the ‘managed opposition’ in Russia
list 2 of 4 Russia seizes assets of French firms, summons UK envoy over Ukraine support
list 3 of 4 Russia’s Novaya Gazeta ‘killed off’ after murders, arrests and pressure
list 4 of 4 Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. In October, authorities searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, and took him in for questioning. Another editor at the paper, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April.
Cofounder Dmitry Muratov addressed journalists who gathered to witness the closure of the Novaya Gazeta office in Moscow.
“Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today,” he said, adding that constitutional guarantees for political and civil rights had “effectively ceased to function”.
Novaya Gazeta was one of the few remaining outlets that openly criticised Russia’s war on Ukraine and the Kremlin’s policies, amid a widening crackdown on the media and free speech.
In September, the outlet was designated a “foreign agent”. Novaya Gazeta said that since then banks had stopped processing the reader donations on which it relied for financial survival.
United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said in October that Novaya Gazeta’s closure was “yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media” in Russia.
The Kremlin played down the closure, saying it was part of “a normal cycle of change”.
The paper was co-founded by former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and funded with money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize. It continued reporting despite censorship tightening in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Several of its reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work, among them Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating abuses by Russia’s military in Chechnya and criticised President Vladimir Putin’s rule.

items.content:
Trump speaks to reporters in the White House press briefing room Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP
Trump speaks to reporters in the White House press briefing room Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP
Trump says US war in Iran ‘effectively over’ as he plays down escalation concerns
President, after talks with Qatari PM, suggests end to war coming ‘fairly soon’ and military escalation not needed
Donald Trump has said that the war in Iran is “effectively over” as he played down concerns that the US would escalate its military campaign against Tehran after the midterm elections.
During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and that an escalation was not needed.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.
The remarks followed talks in the Oval Office with the Qatari prime minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has lobbied Trump alongside other Gulf countries not to resume the fighting against Iran.
“We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon,” he added.
Trump has frequently exaggerated claims about the status of negotiations with Iran, saying a final peace deal was imminent dozens of times during the nearly nine-month long war.
The US had continued to move troops to the Middle East in the run-up to the midterm elections. There was speculation that the Trump administration was waiting for the elections to take place before resuming a military campaign, in order to prevent a backlash at the polls.
Republicans were nevertheless routed in a historic defeat in which they lost both houses of Congress, with the vice-president, JD Vance, declaring soon after that the Iran war was a key reason for the defeats.
Trump earlier on Monday said on Truth Social that the leaders of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait would prefer the “status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History”.
He repeated a mantra that Iran would not be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon, and added that if the situation changed then the US was ready to resume full-scale military action against Iran.
“At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely,” he continued. “Israel, and the entire Middle East, are protected from Iranian danger and threats. We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected. At the conclusion of this Military Engagement, the American People, and the World, will be far safer and more secure.”

items.content:
Rethinking Strategic Stability with China: From Coercion to Constructivism
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
Rethinking Strategic Stability with China: From Coercion to Constructivism
Rethinking Strategic Stability with China: From Coercion to Constructivism
Every administration since the Cold War has been looking for a significant foreign policy breakthrough with China. Spanning containment and normalization to opening and reform , U.S. policymakers have long hoped that China would fulfill its place in the international order and transform itself into a " responsible stakeholder ." Despite years of pivots, new visions, trade arguments and agreements, and other policy swings , the lack of transformational progress is now set against the backdrop of rapidly expanding nuclear capabilities under the leadership of a Chinese general secretary doubling down on authoritarianism and revisionist history . Here, I examine a different factor that generates patterns of behavior in international relations: status recognition. Status is a motivating factor that explains China's perspective and resistance to arms control, and therefore, offers an opportunity to change the outcome of ongoing negotiations. Status recognition, that is, the position and identity of a state reciprocated by other states, is one area of negotiation and compromise that remains untested. Coercive diplomacy has not achieved strategic stability with China, but there are few alternatives in the public discourse. My intent is to provide some new thinking to address an old problem. The theory I present here is informed by academic experience, 20 years as a military officer in a nuclear career field, personal experience at a 2023 P5 meeting with Chinese defense officials, and ongoing affiliation with a long-term Track 1.5 participant. The sections below include a brief description of status, the critical and continuous role status plays in Chinese culture and national identity, and a status-informed approach with recommendations beyond coercion to build a new era of strategic stability. With a third U.S.-Chinese summit fast approaching, preparation for the upcoming meeting between President Donald Trump and General Secretary Xi Jinping is another opportunity to set the stage for the new era they both seek.
Status consists of hierarchy and identity . Each state holds a perception of itself and its position in the hierarchy, and other states validate that position and identity through patterns of behavior and social interactions. There are different organizing principles that generate distinct hierarchies within the international system of states. The distinction between nuclear and non-nuclear states is one organizing principle that results in a recognizable hierarchy. Furthermore, among the nuclear weapon states, there are additional perceptions of positions of authority and influence that affect the relationships between states in the hierarchy. For example, North Korea does not have the same global influence as the United States or Russia. The United Kingdom, France, India, and Pakistan are usually described as regional nuclear powers as opposed to global superpowers or great powers. Perceptions of rank within (or outside) the hierarchy generate interactions that reinforce the rank order in the group. This pattern of state behavior among nuclear powers is relatively stable.
Identity is a state's self-perception in comparison to others . When others do not validate or reciprocate a self-perceived identity, the immediate remedy is to engage in identity-seeking behavior. According to social identity theory, identity-seeking behavior includes emulation, competition, or creativity in order to generate the desired social recognition . Just as individuals rely on others to recognize and reciprocate self-perceptions through social interactions or voluntary deference , states rely on others for validation as well. Social interactions among states generate patterns that reinforce identity throughout the larger system. The presence of a status deficit, defined as a state's dissatisfaction with others' reciprocation of its self-perceived identity and position in a hierarchy , results in status-seeking behavior if the state believes it is possible to reorder the hierarchy and/or reconcile its identity-recognition mismatch. China's observable dissatisfaction with its status , its perception of the existing international hierarchy and its rank in the hierarchy, and China's self-other comparison to the United States, collectively indicate a deficit China is trying to reconcile. It is helpful to understand why.
Understanding China's status deficit requires the observer to set aside the outside-in perspective and examine China from the inside-out. Without an intuitive understanding of the Chinese mindset , it is more difficult to predict behavior, discern common ground, and mitigate one's own biases affecting international relationships. Principally, understanding China requires first and foremost accepting the permanent and collective psychological injury the Chinese people have suffered at the hands of the "foreign other" for a century, and appreciating China's unique needs, concerns, and historical memory spanning thousands of years. Understanding the past exposes how psychological factors and emotion affect China's perspectives and behavior today. The Chinese Communist Party has used its grievance-laden narrative as a powerful identity-building and socially unifying tool to shape Chinese perceptions about the West, preserve the party's legitimacy, and develop renewed Chinese nationalism. China has been doing this for decades, only much more aggressively under Xi .
Just as the West summarily dismissed Putin when he (truthfully) told the world his intentions in 2007, Xi has been sending similar signals for years, and they continue to shape China's behavior . Recent examples from Xi include his speech to the 20th Party Congress in 2022 , the 80th anniversary address commemorating China's victory over Japan , the summary of the May 2026 summit with Trump , and as recently as the summit of the BRICS economic bloc, comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, on September 13, 2026 . In these speeches and in countless others, Xi emphasizes themes of respect and equality of all countries and nations, the importance of the past in building the future, the inevitable rejuvenation and peaceful rise of China, and China's role as a global leader. It is well established that China is uniquely sensitive to status concerns , but now China is growing in confidence and demanding equality and deference as it regains its "rightful" place at the top of the world order .
Evidence of China's status concerns remains consistent in its international agenda and in the short readouts provided by its press releases as well as its national policy on arms control . The May 2026 readout from the U.S.-Chinese summit describes a "new vision" of "building a constructive relationship of strategic stability." The words new, together, cooperation, construct, build, joint, create, mutual, equal, and common are all used by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to describe Xi's perspective of the summit. The language highlights that for China, there is a mismatch between expectation and reality concerning status. If Xi believed China was already an equal partner with the United States, then the readout would reinforce the relationship as it exists and not as a future objective. The language of dissatisfaction in the summit readout represents the status China aspires to obtain.
China is using its expanding military and growing nuclear capabilities to emulate and compete with the United States because they are symbols of status that generate deference in the international system and the nuclear hierarchy. China cannot be a lesser-included if its arsenal is roughly equal to that of the United States, the current ranking member in the hierarchy whose policy and strategy now acknowledge the two-peer reality . U.S. expectations that China pay a social and material price for the permission to participate in arms control negotiations and succumb to coercive pressure campaigns will not succeed. China will not accept America's demands that it preemptively give up the very tools it perceives as critical to generate its aspirational status and deference in the international system.
My own experience at a 2023 P5 meeting illustrates this point. Over two days, it was clear to me that China was not interested in joining existing agreements, institutions, treaties, or other regimes set up without China's input and without equal weight given to China's security concerns. Despite China's obvious position, the proposals by the United States were precisely what China said would not be appropriate, but there were no alternatives to consider at the time. As a first-time observer, it was obvious to me that both sides were entrenched in their respective positions. The United States wanted to bring China into its preexisting ideas of risk reduction, and China would never submit to joining anything it did not help to create. Both immovable, both unwilling to compromise.
More recently, a U.S. participant's personal summary of Track 1.5 dialogues from June 2026 indicates the Chinese position remains the same. China is still communicating that "it is not fair, reasonable, or realistic to ask China to participate at this stage in a so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiation" despite its call in May for "proper limits." The delegation also requested that the United States continue to refrain from responding to China's expanding nuclear proliferation. According to the same participant, China's equally unhelpful suggestions that limit the United States while refusing to limit itself exemplify the importance of perceptions to China. Continuing the existing path, the United States is unlikely to achieve traditional arms control limitations or a grand trilateral agreement based on prior blueprints because it overlooks the unacceptable social patterns of behavior that are so important to China. Status is not the only factor, but these human negotiations are complex, and status recognition is one factor that participants can leverage or manipulate to test a measured outcome.
Exclusive members-only dispatches, premium shows like The Russia Contingency with Michael Kofman, and expert analysis of the conflicts shaping national security.
As preparations are made for the next steps, social identity and status reciprocity are two factors often overlooked in the dominant zero-sum and realist narratives on arms control. China cannot afford to concede valuable leverage before negotiations begin, regardless of how inconvenient that might be for the United States.
China appears to be offering a specific three-year timeframe to negotiate. The first step of a status-informed approach would be for the United States to take the lead and accommodate China's status concerns. The tone should be set from the top and consistent through the foreign policy enterprise and across all dialogues. As many have acknowledged for several years now, the permissive post-Cold War security environment no longer exists . Why is that not evident in ongoing discussions? Historically, China's self-perception of its status is not reflected in the behavior, interactions, and activities of the United States or others in the hierarchy. Rather than issuing proposals that China had no say in creating, the United States could set a new tone, treat China as a peer, and confer the high expectations and responsibilities of a great power accountable to all nations.
China's desired status requires others to reciprocate its identity as an equal great power. Accommodating China's desired status in future dialogues is an approach worth considering and could possibly be at the earliest stages of implementation. After rolling out the red carpet, in U.S. readouts from the May summit, Trump acknowledges that China is one of the two "most important and most powerful countries in the world" and promises that Americans "respect and value" China. It is but one example of Trump making some social accommodations that reciprocate China's desired status in the international order. On the world stage, Trump is validating Xi's perceptions of his nation. Others have noticed the shift as well . This is a positive first step toward the recognition Xi is seeking, but Trump was criticized for "desperately needing Beijing's favor," for his offer of praise, conciliation, and respect , and for his willingness to walk away with little more than the summaries. The pattern of criticism is not surprising when there is nothing tangible to show after such a high-stakes meeting, but perhaps it is not a failure. Perhaps it is indicative of a small, incremental change in behavior from which to build.
Next, the United States should openly demand China contribute at a level commensurate with the status it desires. Deferment is no longer an option for China. The summit readouts' use of the word "constructive" is no accident. Xi called for "healthy stability with competition within proper limits" and said that "the building of a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability should not be a mere slogan, but concrete action taken by both sides toward the same goal." The more recent September readout reiterates much of the same . If China wants to be treated as an equal, then the United States is right to demand that China come to the table with new, concrete proposals to consider. Setting aside the intractable Taiwan issue, the United States should broaden the agenda to look for convergence in a different area and find new common ground. Start by identifying something, anything, both countries can claim as an advantage. For example, rather than using a legacy term like arms control, try starting with a clean sheet or a new multilateral proliferation management or cooperation concept. Look at emerging technology like artificial intelligence, other critical areas like space and cyber, or look at undersea activities as a starting point. Negotiations should refrain from opening discussions with capability limitations or weapons counting until there is a new framework to use and a new (modest) objective to achieve first.
Another idea is to simply consider what Beijing is saying and adjust. Given the long-term predictability of U.S. nuclear forces and an absence of growing nuclear threats to China, its expanding nuclear arsenal might be exactly what it tells the world: a path toward equality. If true, then China should actively demonstrate the reconciliation between its nuclear breakout and artificial intelligence activities with promises of "peaceful development" and "never" engaging in "any form of arms race ." China cannot indefinitely have it both ways. Reciprocating China's social status as an equal great power offers more promise than continuing the practice of inviting it to participate in existing mechanisms that reinforce the superior-subordinate relationship it rejects. This approach could mitigate some of China's identity-seeking behaviors. From China's perspective, continuing its current trajectory is arguably its best option, so what else is there to offer? Status recognition is one step that could enable a new era of strategic stability dialogues rather than allowing old paradigms and beliefs about what success looks like to get in the way of progress.
For those involved, consider an evolution of engagements that do not conform to existing expectations. Any long-term agreement should reflect language that is sensitive to the perceptions it creates. For example, preemptively describing the conditions of reciprocal restraint is conceptually appealing, but given China's firm position against any perception that it is less than an equal great power, it is unlikely to succeed. China is approaching negotiations from a perception of inequality, whereas the United States is approaching from a higher position in the global hierarchy, with reliable external recognition and deference that enables action with near impunity because of its status. China cannot afford to give up its status symbols and compromise its progress like the United States is able to do without equivalent repercussions.
For the domestic audience in the United States, quick political wins for the short-term news cycle are unlikely. The United States should start playing an apolitical and impersonal long game. The only constraints should be new rules that genuinely benefit all parties, not just what U.S. policymakers or the U.S. media think will benefit all parties. Successful negotiations will require creativity and compromise. Starting with a recognition of China's status concerns has a better chance of generating progress than pressuring China to agree to arms control limitations it has more incentives to reject.
The most troubling risk and compelling counterargument to the above approach is that accommodation will look like appeasement. However, conditions in the international system have changed, especially in the era of Xi Jinping, and policy adjustments to these changes are necessary. Accommodating status concerns, which are perception-based, is not the same as appeasement and should not be misconstrued as such. I do not advocate retreat from competition with China, nor do I think the United States should compromise its national security interests or those of its allies and partners. There are choices to be made, though. Hindsight being what it is, how could Putin have been deterred between 2007 and 2014? Consider the parallels of Xi's ongoing commentary. Looking ahead, the United States could simply continue to spend on deterrence, or the United States could continue to spend on deterrence and attempt to make progress by leveraging a multi-layered approach that includes psychology, social identity theory, and status recognition as part of its toolkit.
Constructing a new form of dialogue with an objective to reset the existing pattern of social interaction comes with minimal risk. Status recognition is a negotiation tactic of little cost compared to other bargaining tools. If China really is offering an opportunity to advance an agenda of strategic stability, the United States would do well to discard the social barriers that inhibit creativity and new ideas. If the approach fails, then the immediate result is maintaining the stagnant status quo. For the United States and China to achieve a win-win, the agreement or commitment must be better for both parties than the existing best alternative. It will not be easy. It will take the United States, China, and the global community to create and participate in a new paradigm of major-country relations . Permitting status reciprocity might unlock a more productive era not only in U.S.-Chinese relations, but throughout the international system.
Nicole Klingensmith is a retired Air Force officer with experience in nuclear operations, planning, and policy and a certification in strategic foresight. She has a Ph.D. in international relations from Salve Regina University and currently works as an independent contractor.

Nvidia-based compute is getting scarce and expensive for Chinese AI labs on both of their main routes, buying export-compliant cards and renting abroad, and the Financial Times reports that Nvidia’s own crackdowns are part of the reason. Nvidia has told cloud partners worldwide that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese firms, while Chinese companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation cards this year to cover the shortfall. Meanwhile, a B300 rack that sells for about $600,000 internationally reportedly fetched $2.8 million in China last month.
Chinese customers have ordered more than 6 million of Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX Pro 5500 cards. That is at least twice the 3 million that the company could reportedly manufacture in 2027. One source told CNBC that it was proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront, in comparison to a non-Chinese entity.
Many Chinese groups have relied on overseas leases for advanced AI work, which can include model training, and these tech groups have been the biggest clients for data centers in Southeast Asia. Data centers unable to find non-Chinese clients could be forced to pull back supply, and it’s “difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the US,” one Singapore-based group told the FT . While Nvidia hasn’t confirmed or denied its new rule, implementing it would ease criticism from U.S. lawmakers just as Chinese demand is growing.
What Nvidia told partners has come through verbal instructions, via sales and regional teams, and applies globally rather than just in Asia. Existing deals and leases are not changed, but new ones must comply. Nvidia’s whitelist more than halved its authorized Asian buyer count, which encouraged more Chinese groups to lease over other options, including smuggling. On top of this, Fleet Intelligence tracking is now required for Southeast Asian providers that want to become Nvidia Cloud Partners. All of these combined — whitelist, cap, and tracking — may act to alleviate U.S. concerns.
Among companies that have moved to renting, Moonshot has held discussions to rent capacity from neoclouds that host in Europe with Nvidia GPUs. Specifically, it’s looking for Nvidia Blackwell systems, which export controls bar from China; one source said the talks covered clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs in Europe. These clusters would handle inference, serving models to end users, and the European talks for them happened after the White House said Moonshot accessed Blackwell chips through a facility in Thailand . The firm has been fervent about its intentions to secure more compute.
Moonshot isn't the only Chinese company looking to secure Nvidia chips for AI training. Tencent has a deal with Oracle to lease 100,000 GPUs in Southeast Asian data centers. ByteDance and Alibaba are also pursuing similar long-term leases, and most of these overseas data centers run chips like the forbidden B300. MiniMax, like Moonshot, also leases significant compute both at home and abroad.
The big reason is that domestic AI chip supply is simply not up to the task, although not for a lack of trying. Huawei is expected to hit 1.6 million chips this year, with about 1 million from Alibaba and Baidu, and 300,000 from Cambricon. Total supply this year will be up to 3.5 million, including about 1 million made overseas, against a demand that far exceeds 5 million. That number could more than double next year.
Part of the problem is that the export-compliant cards Chinese firms have been buying , mostly the RTX Pro 6000D, RTX Pro 5000, and RTX 5090, are mostly useful for simpler work such as prefill. Even so, the discontinued 6000D’s pricing in China has reportedly doubled. Huawei’s Ascend 910C outperforms them in most areas, but these lower-end options are still coveted, partly because of a preference for CUDA over Huawei’s CANN. Nvidia’s programming platform is supported by most AI frameworks and libraries, and much in-house code is optimized for it.
Then there’s the RTX Pro 5500 , with 84GB of GDDR7 with ECC and 1,398 GB/s of memory bandwidth. The card runs on a full PCIe Gen 5 x16 interface, draws up to 600 W, and can be split into up to two MIG instances. That still leaves it well short of a B300, which has about 3.4 times the memory and 5.7 times the bandwidth, plus NVLink, which the 5500 lacks.
Export-compliant; samples in December, deliveries from Q1 2027
Licensed by the U.S. case by case; Beijing withholding approval for large-scale imports
Indicated orders from China are not precise, but the total of over six million includes more than three million from ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent. The big three ordered at about $11,400 each, for a total sticker price over $35 billion. This is difficult to fill when there may be fewer than three million produced next year, and partners might only actually get 5% to 10% of the original ask. Starting in 2027, much of Nvidia’s TSMC capacity may shift to Rubin, taking more production, while the RTX Pro 5500’s early samples are due in December.
On the legal side, it’s currently easier to rent than to own as current U.S. law does not give regulators broad authority over overseas cloud access. The Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which would extend U.S. export controls to that area, has sailed through the House but has not yet passed the Senate. Those directly affected — neoclouds and related financiers — price in a possible ban regardless, which drives the upfront premium.
China’s side is not completely clean, either, with about 600,000 H200s reportedly stuck in storage in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to the mainland. Beijing is withholding approvals for large-volume imports such as this. Only relatively small quantities have come in during recent months, for some big internet companies, with others coming through intermediaries and indirect routes in small quantities. The price: over $900,000 for an eight-card H200 server in China at the end of last month, about 3x the cost a year ago. This is despite the fact that H200 sales are already under U.S. license.
The first test that will show how many cards will actually land occurs in Q1 2027, when the RTX Pro 5500 is expected in commercial deliveries. For rentals, whether or not the Remote Access Security Act is a factor depends on a Senate vote, which is not yet scheduled. Nvidia’s Q3 results come in soon, on Nov. 17, which could bring some illumination.
With CEO Jensen Huang under scrutiny lately over reports that he was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy , which Nvidia’s board is now investigating, he’s going to feel the heat even more just a day later, when lawmakers have asked him to attend a closed-door briefing. He’s been pushing for laxer controls and more access, so the assumed 51% rule will also be put to the test.

Processors generating excess heat play a significant part in contemporary data center design, cost, and resource use. However, things could be vastly different if AI chips were more efficient and ran far cooler. South Korean chip startup DEEPX, recently featured by CNBC , thinks its AI chip designs are the answer. DEEPX demonstrated its DX-M1 processor’s cool-running capabilities in a bizarre new dairy-based thermal benchmark. While rival chips caused a knob of butter to sizzle in seconds, atop the DEEPX solution, the butter block remains solid.
Concerns over AI data center proliferation are growing worldwide. These developments are shaping business, the environment, and politics . Some people have very strong feelings about them, and hundreds of people have risked being thrown into jail protesting data centers. The CNBC report linked in the intro looks into why modern data centers are problematic, and indicates that the core issues stem from the use of hot-running processors and the extensive power and cooling apparatus they need.
DEEPX says its simple answer is to “make the AI chips themselves run cooler.” The CNBC video includes a demo of the ultra-low-power DX-M1 processor. In a side-by-side test against unnamed rival AI chips, you can see the DX-M1 NPU is clearly cooler. DEEPX CEO Kim Nok-won claims a temperature difference of 25 to more than 40 degrees Celsius compared with competitors. Kim said the side-by-side chips processed “the same AI workload… and every chip melted the butter except the last chip [DX-M1].”
The dairy-based thermal challenge is certainly eyebrow-raising, but we note some big gaps in the comparison information. Most notable was the question of how fast each processor tackles the test workload. Anyone can run a chip cool if the power and clocks are scaled back. PC enthusiasts undervolt and/or underclock their GPUs all the time for efficiency, better thermals, and reduced fan noise.
DEEPX’s DX-M1 NPU has been produced on Samsung 5nm since August 2025, according to The Elec reports. It has won approximately $13.3M worth of orders thanks to this sliver of silicon. The company is planning to move forward with the next-gen DX-M2 AI chip, which is based on Samsung 2nm , with its mass production aiming for H2 2027.
In conclusion, these NPUs look set for edge computing and robotics applications, so they aren’t really competing in the same space as the racks of power-gulping Nvidia Blackwell and Ruben GPUs featured in the CNBC news feature. Eventually, we might see the hundreds or thousands of hot-running Nvidia GPUs with beefy liquid cooling apparatus get replaced by cooler-running custom accelerators. Such an innovation could cool the backlash against AI data centers . However, DEEPX’s DX-M1 or even DX-M2 chips aren’t going to compete in that space, so this butter test is a bit of a red herring.
The CNBC report also highlights SK hynix’s work on iHBM , a next-gen low-power consumption, and cool-running. The ‘i’ stands for ‘Integrated Cooling Element,’ according to an exec talking to CNBC. CoolIT is also trying a similar approach by bringing water cooling even closer to the heat-generating silicon.

Markets were widely speculating that the president might restart open conflict with Iran after the Republican Party lost to Democrats in the midterm elections.
However, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio made contrasting remarks in Florida before leaving to meet Group of Seven counterparts in Paris, saying Iran's demands so far have proven to be unacceptable and in some cases "outrageous and ridiculous."

Stock Market Correction Or Crash? 3 Charts For The Week Ahead After The AI Sell-Off
Investors are watching for signs that AI infrastructure spending plans remain intact despite the post-election selloff.
A cooler inflation reading could ease pressure on tech stocks, but political concerns around data-center construction remain.
This week's data and company commentary will test whether investors are ready to buy the AI trade's latest pullback.
Wall Street's AI trade lost its footing last week after the midterm election. The Nasdaq ended the week nearly 12% below its October record, officially putting it in correction territory. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 recorded its steepest one-day decline last week since April 2025.
In pre-market trading on Monday, SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was up 0.31%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) moved 1.4% higher. However, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) dipped around 0.40%, and retail sentiment around SPY on Stocktwits improved to 'neutral' from 'bearish' territory over the past day.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
This week's market moves will showcase whether the selloff in AI and semiconductor stocks was a temporary shakeout or the start of a deeper retreat. The outcome for markets is likely to depend on the political outlook for data-center construction, whether investor anxiety begins to ease, and whether inflation gives the Federal Reserve room to hold off on raising interest rates.
Here are three charts that show what to watch this week:
The election has begun to separate potential winners and losers within the AI trade. Companies tied to building and powering data centers came under pressure after Democrats won control of Congress, while clean-energy stocks gained ground.
SMH, VRT, CEG, TAN and S&P 500 price change month-to-date on November 9 as of 4:00 a.m. ET. | Source: Koyfin Investors' concerns center around the fact that AI's expansion depends on more than chips and computing power. It also requires electricity, land, and regulatory approval to build new facilities. Whether the sell-off worsens or eases this week will depend on signals about whether political and local opposition could make data-center projects harder to develop.
Meanwhile, clean-energy companies could benefit if investors expect a Democratic-led Congress to support more renewable-energy development.
Vertiv's (VRT) sell-off last week offers a useful test of whether the recent selling reflects business concerns or a broader shift in investor sentiment. The data-center equipment maker reported strong results and raised its forecast last month. However, last week, the stock fell with no company-specific news to explain the decline. Peers including Eaton (ETN) and nVent (NVT) also fell.
This week's results from CoreWeave (CRWV), Applied Materials (AMAT) and Cisco (CSCO) will also offer another read on customer demand and spending across the AI infrastructure industry.
The VIX Shows Whether Investors Are Worried Or Panicking
Wall Street's fear gauge has climbed to its highest level since April, but its latest reading points to anxiety rather than outright panic.
VIX and VIX to 3-month VIX ratio year-to-date on November 9 as of 4:00 a.m. ET. | Source: Koyfin The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) measures the market's expectation of stock-market volatility over the next 30 days. Readings above 20 generally signal elevated concern, while moves above 30 are often associated with more severe market stress. The index closed Friday near 25.5.
VIX's comparison with its three-month counterpart showed a ratio of 1.0, which signals that near-term corn is elevated. However, it's below the roughly 1.1 reached during earlier bouts of market stress this year. Similar spikes in volatility have often been followed by market gains, although that pattern does not guarantee a recovery this time.
This week, a move back below 20 would suggest market anxiety is easing. A climb above 30 would point to more severe stress and raise the risk of further volatility-driven selling.
As for the VIX ratio, a move above 1.1 would indicate that concern about an immediate selloff is intensifying. Tuesday's inflation report could be a catalyst in either direction. A hotter reading could push volatility higher, while a cooler one could help it recede.
Inflation Report Could Shift December Fed Rate Expectations
The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) report is scheduled to come out on Tuesday and could help determine whether the Federal Reserve faces more pressure to raise interest rates in December. Economists polled by Reuters expect consumer prices to have risen 0.3% in October.
Brent crude oil price and U.S. 2-year Treasury yield, since September, on November 9 as of 4:00 a.m. ET. | Source: Koyfin Following Friday's strong jobs report, traders have priced in roughly an 80% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch data.
Two competing signals are shaping the outlook. Oil prices climbed in October but fell last week to about $98 a barrel. The midterm election results raised hopes that the Iran war could ease. A sustained decline in oil prices would help reduce inflationary pressure.
Bond yields, however, suggest investors are still preparing for tighter monetary policy. The two-year Treasury yield, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed policy, remains about half a percentage point above the upper end of the Fed's 4.00% target range.
Interest rates matter especially for AI stocks. Higher borrowing costs make it more expensive to finance data-center construction, while also reducing the present value investors assign to companies' expected future earnings.

items.title: The Stock Market Is Crashing. History Says the Smartest Investors Are Making This 1 Simple Move. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Stock Market Is Crashing. History Says the Smartest Investors Are Making This 1 Simple Move.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Stock prices are sinking, with more volatility potentially on the horizon.
However, history says the market's long-term future is incredibly bright.
The right strategy can set you up for significant gains over time.
After a brief post-election rally, major stock market indexes are crashing. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +2.35% ) and Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +2.15% ) ended the week more than 5% down from their recent highs, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +2.74% ) entered correction territory by falling nearly 12% from its peak.
The CBOE Volatility Index ( ^VIX -22.31% ) , which is often considered the market's "fear gauge," also increased sharply. The index reached its highest level since March, suggesting that investors are bracing for more volatility in the coming weeks.
The investing moves you make right now can affect your portfolio for years to come, and all of the smartest investors are doing the same thing.
History says this is the single best strategy during a crash
When stock prices are plunging, the temptation is often to sell your investments before the market sinks further. However, it's often safer -- and more lucrative -- to stay invested until the volatility subsides.
The market's short-term performance will always be unpredictable to an extent, and no one can say how long this slump might last. Sometimes, the market will crash only to rebound almost immediately.
This has happened multiple times in the past few years. In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, the S&P 500 lost roughly one-third of its value in a matter of weeks. We saw similar crashes after the "Liberation Day" tariff announcement in April 2025 and earlier this year after the start of the war in Iran .
The investors who suffered the most during those downturns were those who sold their stocks after prices fell. Not only did those investors risk locking in losses by selling a stock for less than they paid, but they also missed out on the lucrative recovery period when the market bounced back.
Investors who continued buying throughout the downturns reaped the greatest rewards. When stock prices fall, it's a prime opportunity to buy quality companies at deep discounts. The market is essentially on sale right now, and the smartest investors are taking this chance to buy more.
Of course, it's not guaranteed that the market will bounce back quickly as it has after recent crashes. But even if we are headed toward a prolonged bear market or recession, staying invested for the long haul is still a lucrative move.
The average S&P 500 bear market since 1929 has lasted 340 days, or around 11 months, according to analysis from Yardeni Research. Some of the most severe downturns in history have also occurred in the last two decades.
The dot-com bubble burst led to the longest bear market in history, lasting two and a half years and surpassing the Great Depression. The financial crisis from 2007 to 2009 was the most severe economic downturn post-World War II, with the S&P 500 losing more than half of its value.
Since January 2000, however, the S&P 500 has earned total returns of more than 700%. If you'd invested $10,000 in the S&P 500 back then and never contributed another dollar, you'd have nearly $82,000 by today.
Market crashes are daunting even for experienced investors, so if you're feeling rattled right now, that's normal. The best thing you can do right now is double-check that you're investing in strong stocks with healthy fundamentals, prepare to hold those investments until the market inevitably recovers, and perhaps consider buying more while stocks are at a discount.
